questions.question: Living things need resources such as food, water, light, space, shelter and mates. When do two living things compete for one of these?
questions.answer: When there is not enough of it for both
choices: When there is not enough of it for both
Whenever they both need the same one
Only when they are of different kinds
Only when the resource is food
questions.context: Competition happens only when a resource is in short supply; where there is plenty for all, sharing it costs no one anything. Members of one species compete too, often hardest of all, since they need exactly the same things, and the resource can be light, water or space as well as food.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade ecology (TEKS 6.12A, NGSS MS-LS2-1) teaches that organisms compete for a resource they share when it is limited.

questions.question: In a desert, seed-eating ants gather seeds by day, and seed-eating rodents gather the same kinds of seeds by night, so the two seldom meet. Seeds there are in short supply. Do the ants and the rodents compete?
questions.answer: Yes, since each seed one eats is lost to the other
choices: Yes, since each seed one eats is lost to the other
No, since they gather at different times of day
No, since ants and rodents never fight each other
Yes, but only when they happen to meet
questions.context: Competition needs no fight and no meeting: each seed one side eats is a seed the other cannot have. When ecologists fenced rodents out of desert plots, the number of ant colonies there rose by 71 percent, and where they took the ants away, the rodents increased.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that competition for a shared, limited food can be indirect, between kinds of animals that never meet.

questions.question: Some kinds of small birds nest only in holes, such as the hollows of old trees. In woods short of such holes, ecologists have put up nest boxes and found more of these birds breeding there. A scarce resource that holds a population's size down, as the holes did, has a name. What is it?
choices: A limiting factor
A carrying capacity
A population density
A habitat
questions.context: A limiting factor is the resource in shortest supply, and it caps a population however much of everything else there is. Here nest holes held the birds' numbers down, so more places to nest meant more birds. Carrying capacity is something else: the largest population a place can support, which its limiting factors set.
questions.grade_note: The limiting factor, a scarce resource that caps how large a population can grow, is named in the 6th-grade interdependence standard (TEKS 6.12A).

questions.question: Wheat needs nitrogen and phosphorus, two nutrients it takes from the soil. A farmer's field has plenty of nitrogen but too little phosphorus, and he spreads extra nitrogen on it. What will set how much his wheat can grow?
questions.answer: The phosphorus, since it is the scarcer
choices: The phosphorus, since it is the scarcer
The nitrogen, since it is more plentiful
Both together, since their total has risen
The nitrogen, since he has added more of it
questions.context: A plant's growth is set by the scarcest thing it needs, not by the total: extra nitrogen cannot stand in for missing phosphorus, and only more phosphorus will help. Justus von Liebig made this idea famous in 1840, and it is often pictured as a barrel that holds water only up to its shortest stave.
questions.grade_note: That the scarcest resource, not the total, caps growth is the core of the 6th-grade limiting-factor idea, and plants taking nutrients from the soil is 6th-grade content.

questions.question: A population of living things that moves into a new home with plenty of food grows fast at first. The largest population that home can support year after year is its carrying capacity. As the population nears that size, what usually happens to its growth?
questions.answer: It slows down and levels off
choices: It slows down and levels off
It speeds up faster than ever
It carries on at the same speed
It stops at once, then crashes to zero
questions.context: As a population fills its home, its members compete harder for what is left, so its growth slows until its numbers level off near the carrying capacity; graphed over time, this makes an S-shaped curve. A population that shoots past the carrying capacity shrinks back, but it does not usually die out.
questions.grade_note: Carrying capacity, and populations levelling off as resources run short, are taught with limiting factors in 6th-grade ecology.

questions.question: The United States Coast Guard released 29 reindeer on St. Matthew Island in 1944. With no predators there, the herd grew to about 6,000 by 1963, and through each winter it fed on the island's lichen, eating much of it away. What happened to the herd next?
questions.answer: It crashed as nearly all of them starved
choices: It crashed as nearly all of them starved
It levelled off at about 6,000
It shrank slowly to a steady size
It kept growing as the lichen grew back
questions.context: The herd had grown far past the island's carrying capacity. When deep snow covered the last of the lichen in the hard winter of 1963 to 1964, the reindeer starved, and by 1966 only 42 were left.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn what happens when a population grows past what its environment can support; St. Matthew Island is a standard documented case.

questions.question: Few small plants grow on the floor of a thick forest in summer, and those that do grow slowly. Which resource do they run shortest of there?
choices: Sunlight
Water
Warmth
Carbon dioxide
questions.context: The tall trees' leaves catch most of the light first, and in summer often less than 7 parts in every 100 of the sunlight reach the forest floor, sometimes less than 1. Light is the limiting factor there, as water usually is in a desert, and the plants that live on a forest floor must be able to grow in deep shade.
questions.grade_note: Plants competing for light, and light as the limiting factor on a forest floor, are standard 6th-grade examples (TEKS 6.12A names the quantity of light).

questions.question: A gardener sows carrot seeds far too thickly, and the seedlings come up packed close together along the row. She leaves every one of them to grow. Compared with carrots spaced a few centimetres apart, what will most of hers be like at harvest?
questions.answer: Smaller, from sharing light, water and nutrients
choices: Smaller, from sharing light, water and nutrients
Larger, from sheltering one another from the wind
The same, since each makes its own food
Larger, from crowded roots loosening the soil
questions.context: Crowded plants of one kind need the same light, water and soil nutrients, so they compete hard and most grow stunted; crowded carrots also twist around one another. Making its own food does not spare a plant from competing, because it needs light, water and nutrients to make it.
questions.grade_note: That plants compete for light, water and soil nutrients is part of the 6th-grade interdependence standard; crowded seedlings are the everyday case.

questions.question: Two kinds of paramecium, tiny one-celled living things, eat the same bacteria. In a lab, each kind does well in a tube of its own. When both kinds share one tube with a limited supply of food, what happens?
questions.answer: One kind dies out, and the other thrives
choices: One kind dies out, and the other thrives
Both kinds live on, sharing the food evenly
Both kinds die out, as neither gets enough
Both kinds do well, just as they did alone
questions.context: Georgy Gause ran this test in 1934: together, one kind kept growing while the other dwindled and died out. Two kinds that need exactly the same scarce resource cannot share it for long, and kinds that live side by side in nature often use different foods or places.
questions.grade_note: Middle-school texts (CK-12 Life Science) teach that when two kinds compete for the same limited resource, the less suited one may move away or die out.
